content: The document outlines various strategies and challenges related to adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) for individuals living with HIV, as well as recommendations for improving care delivery and retention in treatment programs. Below is a professional interpretation of the content: 1. New Recommendations for ART Adherence and Service Delivery: Text messaging is recommended as a tool to promote adherence to ART. Integration of ART services with maternal and child health, tuberculosis (TB), and opioid substitution therapy is encouraged. Decentralization of ART services and task-shifting to other healthcare providers are proposed to improve access and efficiency. 2. Barriers to ART Adherence: The World Health Organization (WHO) defines adherence as the extent to which a person’s behavior aligns with healthcare provider recommendations, including taking medications, following diets, and making lifestyle changes. Sustained adherence to ART is critical for suppressing viral replication, improving immune function, reducing drug resistance, and preventing HIV transmission. Barriers to adherence include individual factors (e.g., forgetfulness, depression, substance use), medication-related factors (e.g., side effects, complex regimens), and health system factors (e.g., frequent clinic visits, long travel distances, and costs). 3. Special Populations and Adherence Challenges: Pregnant and Postpartum Women: Challenges include pregnancy-related conditions (e.g. Adolescents: Infants and Children: Limited pediatric formulations, poor palatability, and reliance on caregivers for adherence pose significant challenges. People with Mental Health Disorders: Depression and other mental health conditions can impair adherence due to forgetfulness and poor comprehension of treatment plans. Substance Use Disorders: Alcohol and drug use can lead to poor adherence due to forgetfulness, disorganization, and competing priorities. 4. Interventions to Optimize ART Adherence: No single intervention is universally effective; tailored approaches are necessary based on individual needs and barriers. Program-level interventions include eliminating out-of-pocket costs, using fixed-dose combination regimens, and strengthening drug supply systems to prevent stock-outs. Individual-level interventions include text messaging, nutritional support, peer support, and management of depression and substance use disorders. Patient education and counseling are essential at ART initiation and throughout treatment to improve adherence and retention. 5. Monitoring Adherence to ART: Effective monitoring requires a combination of approaches, including viral load testing, pharmacy refill records, self-reports, and pill counts. Viral load monitoring is recommended to assess treatment response and failure, but it must be combined with other adherence monitoring tools. Pharmacy refill records can indicate adherence but may overestimate it if patients collect medications without taking them. Self-reports and pill counts are commonly used but may be inaccurate due to recall bias or intentional misreporting. 6. Retention in HIV Care: Retaining individuals in care is critical for optimal health outcomes, especially for those not yet eligible for ART or those who have not initiated treatment. Barriers to retention include high costs, long travel distances, and long waiting times at clinics. Strategies to improve retention include decentralizing services, reducing waiting times, integrating care, and providing family-focused services. Social support interventions, such as peer support and outreach, have shown promise in addressing structural and psychosocial barriers to retention. 7. Special Considerations for Key Populations: Key populations, such as sex workers, men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, and people who inject drugs, face additional barriers to accessing care. Peer-based interventions and non-judgmental, multidisciplinary care approaches have shown encouraging results in improving adherence and retention. 8. Use of Mobile Technology: Mobile phone text messaging is a cost-effective and widely accessible tool for improving ART adherence. It provides reminders and engages individuals in care without requiring significant changes to daily routines. Evidence supports the use of text messaging as part of a broader package of adherence interventions, though privacy concerns and national regulations must be addressed. 9. Nutritional and Financial Support: Nutritional support, such as counseling, food vouchers, and cash transfers, can improve adherence in food-insecure settings. Financial support, including reimbursement for care-related costs, can reduce the burden of HIV care and improve retention in disadvantaged settings. 10. Good Practices for Chronic HIV Care: Health systems need to transition from providing episodic acute care to managing HIV as a chronic condition. Strategies include reorganizing services to reduce waiting times, integrating care, and ensuring uninterrupted ART supply. In summary, improving adherence to ART and retention in care requires a multifaceted approach that addresses individual, medication-related, and health system barriers. Tailored interventions, patient education, and supportive environments are essential for achieving optimal treatment outcomes.
